FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Distinguish low-energy gunshot wounds from high-energy gunshot wounds.
Describe the initial evaluation and workup for gunshot wound injuries.
Discuss the definitive management of gunshot wound injuries.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Firearm-related injuries are common in civilian and military populations, resulting in
substantial morbidity, mortality, and socioeconomic consequences.
Ballistic injuries vary with regard to soft-tissue and bone damage based on the type and
distance of the projectile.




NOTES

AAOS | Gunshot Wounds

1/26

The extremities are the most common location for gunshot wounds (GSWs).

Overview
Ballistic trauma has substantially increased in the past decade, with orthopaedic
procedures being among the most common surgical interventions.1 The extremities are
the most common location of GSWs, and GSWs are associated with fractures in 44% of
patients.2 Fractures resulting from GSWs are a heterogeneous group of injuries requiring
individualized management.
Epidemiology
The incidence of nonfatal GSWs has been increasing.
Most civilian GSWs are caused by low-energy handguns.

Epidemiology
An estimated 535,150 nonfatal GSWs occurred in the United States between 2014 and
2018, an increase of approximately 41% from the previous 5 years.3 Civilian gunshot
injuries are most frequently observed in urban trauma centers but may be encountered
in any locale. Forty-two percent of US adults live in a household with a gun.4 Nonfatal
firearm injuries disproportionately affect males, racial/ethnic minorities, and those
younger than 35 years.5
Mechanism of Injury
Firearm Characteristics
The amount of tissue damage is determined by the physical properties of the bullet (eg, mass,
shape), flight characteristics (eg, velocity, tumble, distance to target), and tissue characteristics
(eg, elasticity; Figure 1 and 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
2/26

Kinetic energy of a bullet is proportional to its mass and its velocity squared (kinetic energy =
0.5 × mass × velocity2).
Handguns deliver low-velocity bullets that travel slower than 2,000 ft/s.
Military and hunting rifles deliver high-velocity bullets that travel faster than 2,000 ft/s.
Shotguns deliver bullets at a low velocity (1,000 to 1,400 ft/s) but may cause high-energy
injuries if fired at close range.
Mechanism of tissue damage
Crush and laceration
Cavitation
Shock wave
Secondary missiles
Low-energy GSWs can be distinguished from high-energy GSWs, which cause profound soft-
tissue destruction, via a thorough clinical examination.
Figure 1 Image shows examples of high- and low-velocity weapons. (Adapted with permission
from Zuelzer DA: Ballistic orthopaedic injuries, from Orthopaedic Trauma Association Resident
Core Curriculum Lectures. Available at https://ota.org/sites/files/2021-
06/Special%20Issues1%20Ballistic%20Orthopaedic%20Injuries.pdf. Accessed February 2, 2022.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
3/26

Figure 2 Schematic drawing shows a bullet traveling along its axis of flight. Yaw (Ψ) is the
oscillation of a bullet around this axis, which influences velocity (via increased drag) and the
orientation of the bullet. (Reproduced with permission from Jabara JT, Gannon NP, Vallier HA,
Nguyen MP: Management of civilian low-velocity gunshot injuries to an extremity. J Bone Joint Surg
Am 2021;103[11]:1026-1037.)

Mechanism of Injury
The amount of tissue damage caused by a projectile is a result of the kinetic energy
transferred to the tissues. Bullet velocity is one of several factors that determine the
amount of energy and subsequent tissue damage (Figure 3). The effect of projectile
mass is amplified in patients with a close-range shotgun injury, in which multiple, high-
mass projectiles generate extensive tissue damage. Projectile design is another factor as
observed with hollow-point bullets, which deform and expand, transferring more energy
to the tissues after impact.
Flight characteristics, including the bullet path and the bullet yaw or tumble (flipping end
over end), also influence the amount of tissue damage. Shots fired at close range impart
more damage than those fired at a distance. If a bullet is retained, its entire kinetic
energy is transferred to the tissues. If a bullet exits through the body, only part of its
kinetic energy is transferred. Bullet yaw increases the surface impact area of the
projectile and results in more of the kinetic energy of the bullet being dispersed to the
tissues.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
4/26

Figure 3 Photographs show gelatin blocks perforated by .30-caliber missiles at less than
1,000 fps (A) and at 2,800 fps (B). Arrows indicate the missile tracks. (Adapted with
permission from Ziperman HH: The management of soft tissue missile wounds in war
and peace. J Trauma 1961;1:361-367.)
Bullets cause direct and indirect damage to tissues. Dense, inelastic tissues, such as
bone and solid organs, are more easily damaged by projectiles than lower density,
elastic tissues, such as lung and muscle. A projectile crushes or lacerates tissue as it
strikes the body, forming a permanent cavity. Temporary cavitation occurs as energy is
distributed away from the bullet path. The damaged area in low-energy GSWs usually is
restricted to the path of the bullet, whereas high-energy GSWs can damage tissue
several centimeters away from the area of impact. In addition, because cavitation is a
negative-pressure phenomenon, contamination can be sucked back into the wound as
the cavitation collapses, contributing to the high degree of contamination in patients
with a high-energy GSW. A shock wave can cause damage to tissues, such as nerves, that
are not in the immediate bullet path. Secondary missiles from metal or bone fragments
result in additional damage.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
5/26

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Initial assessment begins with Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol.
The type of weapon and the proximity of the patient to the weapon should be determined.

Patient History
The type of weapon, the number of rounds, and the proximity and position of the
patient in relation to the weapon should be determined if possible. Firearm injuries may
be self-inflicted or caused by another person. Talking to the patient, first responders,
and law enforcement officers may aid in obtaining a complete patient history.
Physical Examination
A secondary survey that includes a head-to-toe physical examination should be performed.
The skin should be examined for all bullet wounds.
The extremities should be evaluated for the level of soft-tissue injury, swelling, deformity, and
exposed bone.

Physical Examination
Clothing should be removed, and the skin should be thoroughly inspected for all
entrance and exit wounds. Exit wounds may be located some distance away from and
typically are larger and more irregular than entrance wounds. The number of entry
wounds should be equal to the combined number of exit wounds and the number of
retained bullets. A thorough evaluation should be performed to ensure no gunshot
wounds are missed. The size of the bullet wound may not necessarily be associated with
the underlying soft-tissue injury. Neurologic and vascular examinations should be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
6/26

carefully performed and documented. A high index of suspicion for vascular injury
should be maintained in patients with a junctional GSW, such as injuries to the groin and
axilla.7 If concern for vascular injury exists, the ankle-brachial index should be obtained.
CT angiography should be performed in patients with an abnormal ankle-brachial index
(<0.9; Figure 4).
Figure 4 Sagittal CT angiogram of a left leg with a gunshot wound shows a posterior
tibial artery injury. (Courtesy of Mai P. Nguyen, MD, St. Paul, MN.)
Imaging Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
7/26

Radiography
Orthogonal radiographs, including the joints above and below the site of the injury, should be
obtained.
Wounds should be marked with the use of radio-opaque markers before obtaining
radiographs.
Advanced Imaging Studies
CT may be helpful in the evaluation of possible intra-articular bullet fragments and
periarticular and complex fractures.
Management
Emergency Department Management
Many patients with a simple GSW can be evaluated and treated in the emergency department
or in an outpatient setting.
Intravenous antibiotic agents and tetanus prophylaxis should be administered.
Wound care should be provided.
Splinting or skeletal traction should be used as necessary.

Emergency Department Management
Approximately 70% of patients with a GSW seeking medical care arrive via emergency
medical services.5 Most patients with minimal soft-tissue injuries and stable fractures
can be safely evaluated and treated in the emergency department without admission to
the hospital. On arrival to the emergency department, intravenous antibiotic agents
(first-generation cephalosporin or clindamycin if the patient is allergic to cephalosporin)
and tetanus prophylaxis should be administered. Gross contamination is removed, and a
nonadherent dressing is placed. Small wounds usually are left open and cleanly dressed
to allow for secondary healing. Life-threatening intra-abdominal, hollow viscus, or
vascular injuries should be addressed first. Depending on the fracture pattern, splinting
or skeletal traction may be applied as necessary for fracture stabilization.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
8/26

Low-energy GSWs
Infection Prevention
Low-energy GSW fractures managed via antibiotic agents and local wound care are associated
with infection rates of less than 2% in nonsurgically managed fractures and less than 5% in
surgically managed fractures.8
Whether managed nonsurgically or surgically, low-energy GSWs do not require formal
débridement; therefore, they are managed the same as closed fractures if minimal soft-tissue
disruption is present (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Photograph of a leg shows a low-energy gunshot injury associated with a displaced tibial
shaft fracture and a small amount of soft-tissue disruption. (Courtesy of Mai P. Nguyen, MD, St.
Paul, MN.)

Infection Prevention
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
9/26

Low-energy GSWs associated with injuries to soft tissue only, fractures that can be
managed nonsurgically, and an injury traversing a joint without intra-articular pathology
can be safely managed via a single intravenous dose of antibiotic agents followed by
local wound care. The infection rate does not decrease with multiple doses of antibiotic
agents.9,10 Standardized management via this pathway has been suggested to decrease
the risks of bacterial resistance, potential side effects of prolonged antibiotic agent use,
and treatment expenses for patients.9-11
Displaced Articular and Extra-articular Fractures
Surgical indications for reduction and fixation of low-energy GSW fractures are the same as
surgical indications for fractures resulting from blunt trauma.
Infection risk and healing potential associated with a low-energy GSW fracture are similar to
that associated with a low- or moderate-energy blunt fracture.

Displaced Articular and Extra-articular Fractures
Low-energy GSW fractures that meet surgical indications for reduction and fixation are
managed similar to closed fractures resulting from blunt trauma (Figure 6). The skin
edges may be débrided if necessary; however, formal débridement of the deeper soft
tissues is not necessary. Retained bullet fragments need to be removed only if they are
intra-articular, compressing neurovascular structures, or in a symptomatic location.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
10/26

Figure 6 Radiographs of a right hip with a gunshot injury. AP (A) and lateral (B)
radiographs demonstrate a low-energy gunshot injury that resulted in a subtrochanteric
femur fracture. AP (C) and lateral (D) radiographs obtained 5 months after antegrade
intramedullary nailing. (Courtesy of Mai P. Nguyen, MD, St. Paul, MN.)
Intra-articular GSWs
Intra-articular bullet fragments should be removed (Figure 7).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
11/26

Figure 7 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates a gunshot injury of the left hip. The intra-articular
bullet was removed via the anterior Smith-Petersen approach. (Courtesy of Mai P. Nguyen,
MD, St. Paul, MN.)
Routine articular débridement to prevent infection is not indicated.
Patients with associated vascular injury may have a higher risk of infection.
Intra-articular fractures should be managed similar to blunt injuries.

Intra-articular GSWs
Intra-articular bullets should be removed to prevent mechanical wear and lead toxicity.
In patients without a retained intra-articular bullet or an injury warranting acute
management, arthrotomy and débridement are not necessary to decrease the risk of
infection. Arthroscopy may be considered in patients with a GSW through the knee to
rule out intra-articular debris or meniscal pathology.12 Patients with vascular injury
require special attention because they have a higher risk for infection. Intra-articular
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
12/26

fractures should be recognized and managed similar to non-GSW injuries via arthrotomy
or arthroscopy and reduction and fixation, if indicated (Figure 8).
Figure 8 AP radiographs of a knee with a partial articular fracture associated with a low-
energy gunshot wound (A) managed via open reduction and internal fixation with the
use of a buttress plate (B). (Courtesy of Mai P. Nguyen, MD, St. Paul, MN.)
Incomplete Long Bone Fractures
May be managed via limited weight bearing for 6 weeks or via prophylactic fixation (Figure 9)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
13/26

Figure 9 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the knee of a 19-year-old man with an incomplete
distal femur fracture successfully managed via toe-touch weight bearing for 6 weeks. (Courtesy of
Albert V. George, MD, Grand Rapids, MI.)

Incomplete Long Bone Fractures
In most patients with an incomplete long bone fracture associated with a GSW, union
can be achieved without displacement via limited weight bearing for 6 weeks if patients
can comply with weight-bearing restrictions. Displacement from secondary trauma
before union may necessitate reduction and fixation in some patients. Routine
prophylactic stabilization of incomplete long bone fractures is not cost-effective.13
Surgeons should discuss nonsurgical management via limited weight bearing versus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
14/26

prophylactic fixation with each patient so a shared decision can be made with regard to
the treatment plan.
High-energy GSWs
Fractures associated with high-energy GSWs should be managed similar to other open
fractures (Figure 10).
Figure 10 Intraoperative photograph shows a high-energy gunshot tibial shaft fracture (type III
open fracture) with severe soft-tissue damage. (Courtesy of Albert V. George, MD, Grand
Rapids, MI.)
Intravenous antibiotic agents and formal irrigation and débridement in the operating room are
critical to minimize the risk of infection.
Skeletal stabilization is dictated by soft-tissue injury, fracture location, and fracture pattern.
External fixation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
15/26

Intramedullary nailing
Open reduction and internal fixation
Wound closure, skin grafting, and/or soft-tissue coverage are delayed (Figure 11).
Figure 11 Images of the leg of a 35-year-old man who sustained a high-energy gunshot wound
with considerable soft-tissue defect. A, AP radiograph demonstrates a displaced distal tibia
and fibular fractures. B, Intraoperative photograph shows management via intramedullary
nailing of the fractures. The medial traumatic wound exposed the bone and implant. This
Gustilo-Anderson type IIIB open fracture required free flap coverage. (Courtesy of Mai P.
Nguyen, MD, St. Paul, MN.)
An induced-membrane technique and delayed bone grafting are performed as necessary to
manage large defects (Videos 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
16/26

Video 1 Egol KA, Fisher N, Gage M, Konda SR: Treatment of a Segmental Bone Defect Using the
Induced Membrane Technique: The Masquelet Procedure [video]. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/18269__Videos. Accessed February 2, 2022.

High-energy GSWs
High-energy GSWs are associated with severe soft-tissue injuries. Fractures associated
with high-energy GSWs should be managed similar to open fractures via timely
administration of intravenous antibiotic agents and formal surgical débridement.
Thorough débridement should be performed in the operating room, and all devitalized
tissue should be removed to reduce the risk of secondary infection. Local antibiotic
delivery may be considered in patients with severe soft-tissue injuries or large soft-
tissue/bony defects. This can be achieved via antibiotic-impregnated absorbable carriers,
such as calcium sulfate, or antibiotic-impregnated polymethyl methacrylate beads or
spacers. Segmental bone defects can be managed via an induced-membrane technique
and delayed bone grafting.
Transabdominal GSWs to the Hip and Pelvis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
17/26

Transabdominal GSWs are associated with an increased risk of infection because of
contamination from the gastrointestinal tract (Figure 12).
Figure 12 AP radiograph of the pelvis of a patient who sustained multiple low-velocity gunshot
wounds, which resulted in spinal cord injuries, pneumothorax, bowel injuries, and pelvic rami
fractures. Pelvic and abdominal abscesses developed despite management via broad-
spectrum antibiotic agents. (Courtesy of Mai P. Nguyen, MD, St. Paul, MN.)
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic agents are recommended.
Formal débridement is performed if bowel injury and intra-articular contamination are
present.
Extra-articular fractures can be managed via broad-spectrum antibiotic agents alone.

Transabdominal GSWs to the Hip and Pelvis
Transabdominal GSWs to the hip and pelvis are associated with an increased risk of
infection because of potential contamination from the hollow, viscus organs.14SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
18/26

Management requires broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic agents with gram-positive
and gram-negative coverage. If intra-articular contamination is present, surgical
irrigation and débridement via an open approach or arthroscopy should be performed
to decrease the risk of septic arthritis (Resource 1). Transabdominal GSWs in patients
with an extra-articular fracture do not require formal surgical débridement, even in
patients with a bowel injury, and may be managed via broad-spectrum intravenous
antibiotic agents alone.
Complications
Malunion
Fractures associated with GSWs may be highly comminuted, increasing the risk of
malalignment, malrotation, and limb-length discrepancy.
Special attention should be paid to restoration of native length, angulation, and rotation
during intramedullary nailing of comminuted GSW femur fractures.15
Comparative measurements of native length, angulation, and rotation can be obtained from
the contralateral side before preparation and draping.
Nonunion
Many fractures associated with low-energy GSWs result in nonunion rates similar to that of
closed fractures.
Higher rates of nonunion have been observed in patients with tibia or forearm fractures;
however, this is not consistent among all studies.16-20
Nonunion is more likely in patients with substantial soft-tissue damage.
Infection
Increased severity of injury and vascular injury increase the risk of infection.
Tibia and forearm GSW fractures may be associated with an increased risk of infection.

Infection
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
19/26

Bullets are not sterilized by the heat of firing and can introduce additional contaminants
from the objects through which they pass (ie, skin, clothing). Despite this, the risk of
infection is low in patients with a low-energy GSW if minimal soft-tissue disruption is
present. Injury severity, fracture location, soft-tissue disruption, and associated injuries
(eg, vascular injury) affect the risk of infection. Increased rates of infection are associated
with tibia and forearm fractures, with some studies reporting rates similar to those
associated with blunt, open fractures and other studies reporting rates similar to blunt,
closed fractures.16-21
Compartment Syndrome
High index of suspicion in patients with a high-energy injury

Compartment Syndrome
Similar to other open fractures, fractures caused by GSWs may be associated with
compartment syndrome, depending on the energy of injury and whether large vessels
were damaged by the bullet. The leg followed by the forearm are the most common
locations for compartment syndrome. Compartment swelling should be examined on
evaluation, and fasciotomies should be performed as indicated (Videos 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
20/26

Video 2 Konda SR, Behery OM, Crespo A, Egol KA, Kester B: Acute Compartment
Syndrome of the Extremity [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2017. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/18271__Videos.
Accessed February 2, 2022.
Nerve Injury
Most peripheral nerve injures associated with a GSW result from neuropraxia or axonotmesis.
Nerve exploration may be indicated in certain patients, and optimal timing of nerve
exploration is controversial.
A high rate of nerve injury (38% to 50%) is associated with humerus and forearm GSW
fractures21-23 (Figure 13).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
21/26

Figure 13 Radiograph of the arm of a 40-year-old patient who sustained a comminuted humeral
shaft fracture and complete radial nerve palsy from a low-energy gunshot wound injury. The
nerve was found to be in continuity at the time of surgical management. The patient had 100%
recovery of the radial nerve at 6 weeks, and union was achieved via bridge plating. (Courtesy of
Mai P. Nguyen, MD, St. Paul, MN.)

Nerve Injury
Most nerve injuries associated with GSWs result from neuropraxia or axonotmesis and
can be managed via observation. The rate of spontaneous recovery in patients with an
upper extremity nerve injury resulting from a GSW has been found to be as high as 70%,
with a 3- to 9-month time frame for recovery.22 Nerve injuries may result from contusion
and/or laceration, with no reliable method to distinguish between types of nerve injuries.
The optimal timing of nerve exploration is controversial, with advocates for acute and
delayed exploration. Acute exploration should be considered in patients with a vascular
injury, patients with a high-energy wound, and patients undergoing surgical fracture
fixation. If electrodiagnostic and clinical signs of nerve recovery have not occurred by 3
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Gunshot Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001081
22/26

months, exploration should be considered. Reasons for persistent nerve malfunction
include nerve rupture or scar tissue entrapping the nerve.
Lead Toxicity
Retained intra-articular bullets may result in lead synovitis and arthritis and systemic toxicity.

Lead Toxicity
The lead in bullets is soluble in synovial fluid, which may result in lead synovitis and
arthritis and, possibly, systemic plumbism. Symptoms of lead toxicity include fatigue,
headache, abdominal pain, nausea, anemia, renal failure, encephalopathy, and
peripheral neuropathy. The risk of systemic toxicity from retained extra-articular bullets
is otherwise low because they become encased by avascular fibrous tissue.24
